triples.rationale: Eliphaz portrays the ungodly person's life as anxiety. Isaiah pictures the unjust as wave-tossed and unable to rest, and declares no rejoicing for the ungodly. Both associate wrongdoing with unrest, but the prophetic statement does not prove Eliphaz's insinuation that Job's suffering establishes his guilt.

triples.relationship: Speech and silence in the experience of pain
triples.rationale: Job says that if he speaks he will not feel pain from the wound and asks how silence would leave him any less wounded. The psalm reports that silence renewed the speaker's pain before he spoke. Both set the decision to speak against the inability of silence to remove distress; Job's conditional statement about speaking is preserved rather than changed to its opposite.

triples.relationship: Appeal to a witness beyond human observation
triples.rationale: Job claims a witness in the heavens and one who knows with him in the highest places as he seeks a hearing. Paul calls God his witness to the unceasing remembrance expressed in his prayers. Both appeal beyond human observation for knowledge of the speaker's case or inward practice. Job's witness remains unnamed; this comparison does not identify that figure as Christ, an angel, or Paul's explicitly named witness.

triples.rationale: Job calls death his father and decay his mother and sister within his lament about Hades as his house. Proverbs tells the learner to call wisdom a sister and acquire understanding as a familiar companion. Both express closeness to an abstract reality through family language, with Job's desolate association with death contrasted with the instruction to embrace protective wisdom; these are not claims about literal relatives.

triples.relationship: Dispossession of houses in judgment language
triples.rationale: Bildad says that the unjust person's house will not be preserved and that others will live in what was his. Jeremiah announces that houses, fields and wives will be transferred to others when the Lord stretches out His hand against the land's inhabitants. Both portray judgment through loss of the household to others; Jeremiah does not verify Bildad's application to Job, and neither passage is rewritten as a claim about absent descendants.

triples.relationship: The lost crown as an image of humiliation
triples.rationale: Job says that glory has been stripped from him and the crown taken from his head. Lamentations declares that the crown has fallen from the community's head. Both portray lost dignity through the crown's removal, but Lamentations' explicit confession of sin is not transferred to Job or used to identify his crown as a literal royal office.
triples.source_text: He stripped glory from me and took the crown from my head.

target_units.text: The crown fell from our head; woe indeed to us, for we sinned!

triples.relationship: Becoming foreign within one's own close circle
triples.rationale: Job says that the neighbors of his house and his maidservants regard him as a foreigner. The psalm's speaker has become estranged from his brothers and a foreigner to his mother's sons. Both express painful alienation from people who should be close through foreigner language; the household members and causes are distinct, and neither statement establishes a change of ethnicity.

triples.relationship: The overthrow of a house in retributive wisdom
triples.rationale: Zophar wishes for destruction to drag the ungodly person's house away on a day of wrath. Proverbs says that the Lord pulls down the houses of the insolent while establishing a widow's boundary. Both connect wrongdoing with the loss of a house, but the proverb's principle does not establish Zophar's accusation against Job or identify either statement with the prologue's house collapse.
